newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian metal supply stable but investment needed.
newsitem.headline: Russian metal supply stable but investment needed.

text.p: The flow of Russian industrial metals to the West looks secure in 1997 as plants keep churning out material despite mounting debts, Western traders and analysts said on Monday.
But they said Russia still needed to attract investment to guarantee its long term survival as one of the world's biggest exporters of nickel and aluminium.
Non-ferrous metals data from the State Statistics Committee painted a relatively stable picture of the country's domestic base metals industry.
Nickel output fell three percent in 1996 from 1995 levels, aluminium rose three percent and copper production increased seven percent, according to the data obtained by Reuters.
The committee gave no outright figures but the percentage change data was in line with analysts' expectations.

"Personally, I am forecasting flat nickel production in 1997," said Jim Lennon, metals analyst at Macquarie Equities in London. "They may even edge higher as there seems to be an effort to pump up production a bit."
A senior physical dealer at a Western trading firm said aluminium output would also remain stable. "I think Russia will continue to crank it out for the forseeable future," he said.
The West depends heavily on Russia's aluminium and nickel exports, and fluctuations in production and deliveries overseas can seriously unnerve markets and swing prices.
Russia accounts for 15 percent of the world's aluminium output and even more of its nickel supply.

The short term export outlook looked steady for nickel, analysts said, because Russian domestic metal demand was unlikely to recover quickly from the slump which has more than halved Russian industrial output since 1992.
Nickel consumption in Russia this year may even shrink as demand from its biggest users, stainless steel mills, weakens.
"Russian nickel demand appears to be falling again," Lennon said. "There appears to be a shortage of ferrochrome at Russian stainless steel mills...Exports may rise slightly as a result."
Russia exports the bulk of its nickel production, which Lennon pegged at around 190,000 tonnes in 1996.
But the longer term outlook for the Russian nickel industry is less certain. "Russian nickel needs reinvestment just to stand still," said one Western nickel expert.
The country may find it hard to attract the vast sums it needs when billions of dollars are already pouring into the huge Voisey's Bay nickel project in Canada.

"Most of the nickel projects going ahead or being talked about are outside of Russia. It is therefore highly probable that some of the existing Russian nickel operations will have a hard time," the expert said.
Russian aluminium supply looked secure in the short term, according to Adam Rowley, also of Macquarie.
He forecast output for the Commonwealth of Independent States would rise to 3.20 million tonnes this year from 3.17 million in 1996. Russia accounts for 90 percent of CIS output.
There are signs that while volumes remain flat, earnings could rise as the quality of Russian aluminium exports, used in a range of industries from packaging to car parts, improves.
"What we are seeing is that the quality of material (coming from Russia) is improving as smelters get their acts together and team up with Western technology," one trader said.
Macquarie's Rowley saw improved Russian aluminium quality narrowing discounts for Russian material against Western brands.
"Russia used to be a source of cheap aluminium, but that is no longer the case," he said.
For copper, the Fleming's Global Mining Group's Commodity Companion forecast CIS copper exports to slip to 580,000 tonnes in 1997 from 610,000 tonnes in 1996.
